teaser.text: Agnico Eagle Mines turns gold-bearing rock into metal and sells it to wholesale buyers. To understand its business, follow the dollar from rock, through processing and sale, to the costs that keep mines running.

blocks.heading: Where could Agnico Eagle Mines' shares be?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast points to C$229.28 in October 2027, down 14%, and C$227.75 in October 2029, down 13%, hinging on gold margins, Barnat’s recovery, project execution and valuation multiples.
The forecast assigns 30% probability to the bear case, 50% to the base case and 20% to the bull case. The base case ends at C$211.28 in October 2029; the bear and bull cases span C$96.32–C$466.06.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Agnico Eagle Mines, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base case takes EBITDA from $9,600 million in 2027 to $8,762 million in 2028. It reaches $8,520 million in 2029. Gold eases from Q2 levels, while production stays near management’s 3.3–3.5 million ounce guidance. Barnat limits output before remediation helps. The bear path bottoms at $4,670 million in 2028 because gold falls and Barnat losses persist. The bull path reaches $13,410 million in 2029 because firm gold and execution lift margins. Each path uses a $450 million annual corporate-cost calibration.
The view would move toward the bear case if gold normalizes during 2027–2029, Barnat fails to replace lost ore during 2027–2028, or Hope Bay spending rises before production.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Agnico Eagle Mines really make?

paragraphs.text: Agnico’s free cash flow subtracts capital spending from operating cash. A stricter view also deducts lease payments and stock-based pay, because both represent economic claims on cash or value. This is an analytical measure, not a separate bank account.

blocks.heading: How much does Agnico Eagle Mines pay per share over time?

paragraphs.text: The dividend starts at $1.80 per share after the quarterly rate reached $0.45. The base case holds $1.80 before rising to $2.00. The bear case cuts it to $1.60 and then $1.20. The bull case raises it to $2.00 and then $2.40. Stability is supported by the four-year $1.60 history, but construction competes with shareholder returns.

In the early years, Agnico paid out more than its internally generated free cash flow while absorbing major acquisitions and debt. By 2025, the pattern had changed: the company had repaid debt, built net cash and left a much larger surplus after dividends and buybacks. It also raised the quarterly dividend to US$0.45 per share and authorized up to US$2 billion for buybacks. Authorization is capacity, not money already spent.

blocks.heading: Does Agnico Eagle Mines cover its dividend with cash?

paragraphs.subsection: 3.4 — The Kirkland Lake merger and per-share value creation
paragraphs.text: Reserves held up better. Reserve ounces per 1,000 shares rose from roughly 105 in 2021 to 110 in 2025. Cash improved more sharply: free cash flow per diluted share rose from about US$1.73 to US$8.67. Dividends plus buybacks per diluted share increased from about US$1.27 to US$2.80. Higher gold prices and later acquisitions contributed, so these results cannot be credited to Kirkland alone.

blocks.heading: What is Agnico Eagle Mines’ dividend yield against its share price?

paragraphs.text: Production edged down in 2025 while realized price rose sharply, widening the realized-price-to-AISC margin to US$2,115 per ounce. Agnico's free cash flow per share rose from US$1.73 in 2021 to US$8.67 in 2025, while net cash replaced net debt. The valuation carries a 4.6% free cash flow yield and a 1.0% dividend yield, but the weighted case shows a negative return through October 2029.

The probability-weighted price is CAD 229.28 in October 2027, implying a 14% negative return including dividends. It falls to CAD 215.99 in October 2028, then recovers to CAD 227.75 in October 2029. The 2029 range is unusually wide: CAD 96.32 in the bear case to CAD 466.06 in the bull case, versus today’s CAD 269.83.

blocks.heading: What has Agnico Eagle Mines guided for 2026?

paragraphs.text: Management expects 2026 production to remain within its stated range, but Barnat has pushed the likely result toward the low end. Guidance is the company’s operating plan for production, costs and investment. Agnico still guides to 3,300–3,500 thousand ounces, while warning that the interruption at Barnat, part of Canadian Malartic in Quebec, will reduce output.

The company has kept its group cost targets, even though Canadian Malartic is expected to have cash costs of about US$1,260 per ounce. Cash cost measures the operating cost of producing an ounce after credits from other metals. All-in sustaining cost, or AISC, adds the capital and corporate spending needed to keep current mines operating, but not the full cost of building future mines.

blocks.heading: Has Agnico Eagle Mines kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Promises are best tested against dated forecasts. Agnico’s 2025 production guidance, meaning its current forecast range, was 3.30–3.50 million ounces after an earlier reduction of about 3%. It ultimately produced 3,447,367 ounces. Meeting the revised range is useful evidence, but it does not erase the earlier change. Porter also said Agnico had returned approximately 48% of free cash flow to shareholders through the first half of 2026 against a target of approximately 40%.

blocks.heading: What is Agnico Eagle Mines’ revenue and profit trend?

paragraphs.text: Revenue rose year over year because the realized gold price increased, while gold production declined. Revenue also fell from Q1, so the latest quarter interrupted the recent upward sequence even as it remained much stronger than the comparable quarter.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Agnico Eagle Mines’ next results?

paragraphs.text: The next decisive evidence will be Barnat’s restart, Hope Bay’s updated study and Odyssey’s shaft production. Agnico plans to release Q3 results on October 28, 2026, after management expected Barnat remediation in Q3 and a mining restart in Q4.
